Woodstock
WOOD-stok
proper noun (Boomer slang)
The Woodstock Music and Art Fair, billed as "3 Days of Peace & Music," held August 15–18, 1969, on Max Yasgur’s dairy farm in Bethel, New York — about forty miles from the town of Woodstock that gave it its name. Roughly 400,000 people came; rain turned the field to mud; food and sanitation failed; and Jimi Hendrix played "The Star-Spangled Banner" in the closing set on Monday morning. Joni Mitchell’s song "Woodstock" (1970) sang of getting "back to the garden." The name became shorthand for the whole counterculture: "the Woodstock generation."

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Woodstock is the festival of August 1969 — three days, nearly half a million young people, rain, mud, music, drugs, nudity, and a remarkable peace — and it became the name for the whole Boomer counterculture. "He’s a Woodstock kid." The Christian observation: Woodstock’s anthem said the quiet part out loud. The young people of 1969 believed they had to "get back to the garden" — to recover an Eden of innocence, nature, and love. Scripture agrees that we were made for a garden and lost it, and it explains why the gate cannot be opened from our side: "So he drove out the man; and he placed at the east of the garden of Eden Cherubims, and a flaming sword which turned every way, to keep the way of the tree of life" (Gen 3:24). Woodstock tried to walk back in on music and marijuana, and found mud. The Babel-builders had a similar plan: "let us make us a name" (Gen 11:4) — a city built by human unity. John’s summary fits the festival: "the lust of the flesh, and the lust of the eyes, and the pride of life, is not of the Father, but is of the world" (1Jn 2:16). Yet the longing was right. The way back to the tree of life has been opened, not by a festival but by a cross, and the Bible ends in a garden-city: "Blessed are they that do his commandments, that they may have right to the tree of life, and may enter in through the gates into the city" (Rev 22:14). A grandparent who was there in the mud can be told: you were right that we need to get back to the garden. There is only one Gate.

Webster 1828 Definition

The festival of August 15–18, 1969 (Bethel, NY; about 400,000 attending) and shorthand for the Boomer counterculture — whose anthem longed to get "back to the garden," a gate Scripture says only Christ reopens (Gen 3:24; Rev 22:14).

WOODSTOCK, n. (proper; 1969) The Woodstock Music and Art Fair, August 15–18, 1969, Bethel, New York; by extension the late-1960s counterculture as a whole. Woodstock generation, Woodstock Nation.

Decode for families: about 400,000 attended; millions now remember being there. Ask your grandparents gently.

Key Scripture

Gen 3:24 — "So he drove out the man; and he placed at the east of the garden of Eden Cherubims, and a flaming sword which turned every way, to keep the way of the tree of life."

Gen 11:4 — "And they said, Go to, let us build us a city and a tower, whose top may reach unto heaven; and let us make us a name, lest we be scattered abroad upon the face of the whole earth."

1Jn 2:16 — "For all that is in the world, the lust of the flesh, and the lust of the eyes, and the pride of life, is not of the Father, but is of the world."

Rev 22:14 — "Blessed are they that do his commandments, that they may have right to the tree of life, and may enter in through the gates into the city."

Heb 10:25 — "Not forsaking the assembling of ourselves together, as the manner of some is; but exhorting one another: and so much the more, as ye see the day approaching."

Modern Corruption

Woodstock sought a return to Eden through music, drugs, and human unity; Scripture shows the garden’s gate guarded by a flaming sword and opened only by Christ.

expand to see more

Woodstock has been mythologized more than any event of its era: half a million young people in peace, sharing food, helping strangers, enduring rain together. Some of that was true and admirable. But the myth leaves out the overdoses, the medical tents, the exploitation, and the fact that four months later the Altamont concert in California ended in violence and death. The garden could not be reached by the road they took. Babel teaches the same lesson: human unity without God builds a tower, not a gate (Gen 11:4).

The longing itself deserves honor. Joni Mitchell’s line about getting back to the garden names the deepest ache of every human heart, and Scripture shares it. The church, too, is a great gathering of the young and old who have left the world to come together — "not forsaking the assembling of ourselves together" (Heb 10:25) — and its gathering points to the true garden-city at the end of the Bible, where the tree of life stands open to those washed in the blood of the Lamb (Rev 22:14).

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Old English wudu (wood) + stoc (a place) → Woodstock, New York (an artists’ town) → August 1969 festival (held at Bethel) → byword for the counterculture.

expand to see more

Old English wudu — wood, forest; stoc — a place, an outlying farm

Woodstock, New York — a Catskills artists’ colony that lent the festival its name

August 15–18, 1969: festival held on Max Yasgur’s farm, Bethel, NY

1970: Joni Mitchell’s "Woodstock" ("back to the garden"); the documentary film

December 1969: the Altamont concert, often called the counterculture’s end

"To keep the way of the tree of life (Gen 3:24)."
